summary: Describes an NSIS quality-of-service model for networks using Resource Management in Diffserv (RMD), which adds admission control and preemption. Edge nodes signal reservations and overload notifications. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A club doorkeeper who counts guests so it doesn't overflow, and tells the front when it's too crowded.

questions: rmd qos model resource management diffserv
subtitle: Scaling QoS reservation across IP networks with lightweight edge-controlled signaling.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services (Diffserv) networks offer QoS classes but lack a standardized way for external devices to dynamically request resources or learn what is available. Per-flow resource management at every router does not scale to large networks with many flows.
tldr.mechanism: RMD (Resource Management in Diffserv) adds admission control by concentrating per-flow tracking at edge nodes (Ingress and Egress routers) while interior routers maintain only per-class aggregate state. Edge nodes signal resource requests intra-domain using lightweight stateless or reduced-state processing, minimizing impact on interior node performance.
tldr.outcome: Networks can dynamically reserve bandwidth for individual flows while keeping interior routers stateless and responsive. The architecture handles severe congestion from link failures by detecting overload and terminating lower-priority flows, enabling QoS guarantees at scale.

today: RFC 5977 is Experimental. RMD-QOSM provides a scalable approach to QoS signaling in Diffserv networks but has seen limited deployment. The specification remains on the Experimental track and has not advanced to Standards Track.

sections.title: The RMD Concept: Scalable QoS for Diffserv Networks
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) provides QoS by marking packets with a DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) and forwarding them according to their class. However, standard Diffserv has no admission control: it cannot prevent the network from being overbooked or guarantee that a flow will get the quality it needs. RMD (Resource Management in Diffserv) extends Diffserv by adding dynamic admission control.

The RMD-QOSM brings RMD into the NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling) QoS signaling framework. The key design choice is to concentrate per-flow state at the domain edges and minimize state in the interior. Edge routers (Ingress and Egress nodes) maintain per-flow information and conduct signaling. Interior routers maintain only aggregated, per-traffic-class state or none at all. This makes the interior highly scalable.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every router tracking every user's data and needs, only the entry and exit routers do that. In between, routers only count 'how many people are traveling in this class?' This keeps the middle simple and fast.

sections.title: Edge-to-Edge Architecture with Stateless Interior Nodes
sections.content:
An RMD domain has four kinds of nodes: QNI (QoS Initiator, external), QNE Ingress (entry to the domain, stateful), QNE Interior (middle, stateless or reduced-state), and QNE Egress (exit, stateful). The end-to-end QoS request arrives at the Ingress, which creates an RMD-QSPEC (a local QoS specification) and sends it via a separate intra-domain signaling path through the Interior nodes. The original RESERVE message is forwarded in parallel to the Egress and onward to destinations.

Interior nodes are stateless or maintain only per-PHB (Per-Hop Behavior) aggregated state, not per-flow state. This minimizes memory use and processing overhead. Edge nodes store the per-flow context and bind the intra-domain reservation (which operates on aggregates) to the per-flow end-to-end reservation. When a failure or reroute causes severe congestion, the Egress detects it and signals the Ingress, which can drop or degrade lower-priority flows to recover capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry gate checks you in by name and records your details. The exit gate checks you out by name. In between, guards just count 'business travelers in car 3, tourists in car 4,' without knowing who you are. If too many business travelers show up, the entry gate can stop admitting more.

sections.title: Admission Control Methods: Reservation-Based and Measurement-Based
sections.content:
RMD offers two main admission control approaches. The reservation-based method has each Interior node maintain one reservation state per traffic class (PHB). When a flow is admitted, its bandwidth is added to the class's reserved total. The Ingress aggregates flow requests into class reservations and signals changes to the Interior nodes.

The measurement-based method uses real-time traffic measurements instead of stored state. In one variant, Diffserv-aware (but not NSIS-aware) Interior nodes count current traffic per PHB and use the signaling messages themselves as probe packets. If congestion is detected, the DSCP of the probe is re-marked to signal the edge that traffic is building up. In another variant, NSIS-aware Interior nodes measure live traffic against a threshold per PHB and admit or reject flows based on current conditions, without storing per-flow records. The measurement-based approach trades some admission accuracy for near-zero state overhead at Interior nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Reservation method: 'We reserved 100 Mbps for business, 50 Mbps for tourists. A new tourist flow needs 10 Mbps, so we have 40 left. OK, admit it.' Measurement method: 'Tourists are using 45 Mbps right now. New flow wants 10? We'd hit 55, which might be too much. Reject it.'

sections.title: Signaling Operation and Message Flow
sections.content:
When an external QNI sends a QoS RESERVE request, the RMD Ingress node creates a local RMD-QSPEC based on the request and sends it via a stateless intra-domain path using GIST Datagram mode (unreliable, no per-flow state). This RMD-QSPEC carries traffic parameters, the PHB class, and admission priority. Each Interior node processes the RMD-QSPEC using its configured method (reservation or measurement) and either admits or marks a failure bit. The message continues to the Egress regardless.

The Egress sends back an intra-domain RESPONSE with the admission status. If all nodes admitted it, the Ingress forwards the original end-to-end RESERVE downstream. If admission failed, the Ingress rejects the request. The binding between per-flow end-to-end state and per-aggregate intra-domain state happens at the Edges using session matching. If severe congestion occurs (e.g., after a link failure), the Egress detects queue buildup and sends a congestion notification to the Ingress, which can trigger release or re-marking of low-priority flows to free capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Entry gate sends a form saying 'one person, 10 Mbps, priority 2.' Each interior stop checks: 'Can we fit this?' If yes, the form keeps going. If no, we mark it but keep going. Exit gate confirms what happened. If everything is full, exit tells entry to stop admitting priority-2 people.

sections.title: Handling Severe Congestion and Network Failures
sections.content:
A severe congestion situation occurs when a link fails and rerouted traffic floods an Interior node with far more load than it can handle. Standard admission control cannot help because the flows were admitted before the failure. RMD includes a severe congestion handling mechanism. When an Interior node or Egress detects that its queue is critically full, it sets a flag in the RMD-QSPEC.

Two strategies are defined. The refresh-based approach uses periodic refresh messages: when the Egress detects congestion, it notifies the Ingress, which responds by pausing refreshes for low-priority flows, allowing their reservations to age out and release capacity. The proportional data packet marking approach re-marks packets from low-priority flows to a lower DSCP, causing downstream routers to drop them preferentially, freeing capacity. Once capacity recovers, the Ingress can re-establish the flows at a suitable quality level.
sections.plainLanguage: If a tunnel floods because another tunnel failed and all its traffic rerouted here: either (1) the exit tells the entry to stop refreshing the least important travelers, so they eventually leave, or (2) we start marking low-importance people with a 'drop me if crowded' badge so other nodes drop them. When the flood stops, we admit them again.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Threat Mitigation
sections.content:
RMD signaling messages may traverse untrusted network paths and could be intercepted or forged. An attacker could claim to be a high-priority flow, flood a network with admission requests, or forge congestion notifications to trigger unwanted flow terminations. The RFC recommends reliance on the security and reliability of the bound end-to-end NSIS session (which runs in parallel at the Edges) and the GIST Datagram mode's inherent limitations on state creation.

The RFC also emphasizes that implementations should follow the security practices of the underlying NSIS QoS-NSLP (RFC 5974) and QSPEC (RFC 5975) specifications. Operators should configure local policies to restrict which flows can claim high priority and should ensure that Interior nodes do not build persistent state that could be exploited for denial-of-service. The use of per-class aggregate state rather than per-flow state at Interior nodes naturally limits the surface area for state exhaustion attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad people could fake being high-priority or create fake congestion alerts. The system defends by only trusting signaling from the entry and exit gates, which verify each other. Interior nodes keep minimal state so they can't be overwhelmed by fake requests.
